title: Tony Jackson, Gypsy Schaeffer's and the Tuxedo shooting
summary: Walking with Stale Bread to hear Tony Jackson, Williams witnesses a gunman run out of the White Rock Saloon and the killing of the man who ran the Tuxedo.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Nickel was a big thing in them days. Yeah. Well, listen, the only thing I can tell you about, when I, I'll use the expression bumming for the meal, stale bread. Why, we used to go around and listen to Tony Jackson.
Yeah. He was waiting for Gypsy Shafer. So on our way back, the second street, the next street behind Basin used to be called Franklin. They've changed it now, I understand.

Crozat is what it's called now, but that's, it used to be Franklin. So we got, we walked back, I met Tony Perini, but I didn't know him that day. Yeah. He used to come around and listen to him. And Tony Jackson played a marvelous piano, he could sing like a woman. And when I was at Omaha, he wrote Pretty Baby, when I was at Omaha I picked up a copy of music of Some Sweet Day, had to go to color shows. See up in New York, people that had to go to color shows, they couldn't go to white. Beautiful number. Some sweet day I'm going to find somebody. And I want to get things right. Yeah, so we left, we left, we sat outside of Gypsy Shafer and listened to him play. So we got to Franklin, Basin, Pop Torres on Basin in Bienville. Across the way from the Broadway, of course Lil Weiss was next door. Buddy Ford, the detective got killed in the Broadway, you see. But I'm getting away from my story, I want to finish. When we got to the corner of Franklin and Bienville, we seen a fellow run out from across the street, who was called the White Rock Saloon. He had a gun in his hand. It seemed like at the 101 hand, Tuxedo sent the dip of blood, come down. I grabbed me and I said, come on, those small blocks, so we went down and popped over. I laid down and we heard the shooting. I don't know which one of the Parker boys, it was Frank and Harry. And the guy run the Tuxedo, he was killed. So that's that one.
That was a very sensational case in those days. Oh yeah, they closed everything down, I've heard.

My teacher was working that night, I had a music teacher who worked on Franklin Street. They called him Hoss, I don't know if you remember him, he's from across the river. Fess they called him, you know, Professor Mineta. Oh yes, yes. Yeah, and he and Peter Bocards were telling me about it.
